title: Warsh asks whether AI changes the rate of discovery as well as the cost of production
summary: Chairman Kevin Warsh opened the Productivity and Jobs Task Force conference by asking whether advanced AI could accelerate the discovery of ideas. Earlier general-purpose technologies supported decades of follow-on innovation. His proposed distinction is that this technology might also automate part of the process of inventing. Ideas are costly to discover but can be used by many people at once. An increase in their production could therefore change potential growth as well as the level of output. Warsh framed that as a possibility requiring evidence. He said recent productivity gains had yet to establish a decisive and lasting break from the past.

The historical comparison sets a high bar. Warsh cited research suggesting that research effort had grown more than twentyfold since the 1930s even as the productivity of that effort had declined. More spending on research, computing or data centres cannot by itself demonstrate an increase in the productivity of discovery. The relevant question is whether more valuable ideas appear per unit of effort, diffuse into actual production, and continue to do so over time. Slower population growth makes the question consequential because fewer potential idea producers could otherwise constrain the rate of discovery.

The staff’s scenarios separate output, employment and asset prices. In the first, improved productivity benefits workers and owners of capital, growth stays above its longer-run average and the economy remains close to full employment. In the second, growth also rises but displacement and frictions keep some workers out of productive jobs. The same positive aggregate GDP outcome can therefore accompany sharply different labour-market conditions. In the third, returns disappoint after investment and equity valuations have risen. A reversal in valuations then accompanies a slowdown and higher unemployment, with recovery eventually taking place without the hoped-for productivity gains. The scenarios assign no probabilities, timing, projected rate path or numerical productivity uplift.

Warsh also raised the possibility of risks to critical infrastructure and stressed human responsibility in the deployment of these tools. His stated role for the Fed was to prepare for changes in potential output, employment and financial conditions. The remarks announce neither a policy action nor a recommendation for the next meeting. Their relevance to rates runs through the future data that could distinguish a lasting supply expansion from an investment boom or an uneven labour transition.

questions.question: What would establish a sustained improvement in the productivity of discovery?
questions.detail: Compare research inputs, commercially adopted innovations and output per hour across cohorts of early and late adopters. Allow time for integration. A rise in investment before output per input improves is consistent with more than one of the scenarios.

questions.question: Can stronger GDP conceal a deterioration in the allocation of labour?
questions.detail: Follow displaced workers’ employment duration, wages and occupational transitions alongside aggregate output and profits. Separate temporary search time from persistent losses. Stable aggregate employment can mask unequal effects across groups.

questions.question: How would a disappointment in AI returns propagate?
questions.detail: Compare actual revenues and utilisation against contracted investment costs, financing needs and equity valuations. Check whether repricing stays concentrated among project sponsors or transmits to credit availability and non-technology activity. Such evidence would help discriminate a financial reversal from a change in measured productivity.
